Parity gaps that remain: `s2_expert_grouped_parity` (the s2 path), `kv_hybrid_parity`'s last step on the XMX kernel, `ple_parity` and `native_expert_parity` need model files. **Fixed bugs worth knowing if you see the symptom** (fixed long ago; the symptom is listed so a search finds this line). `--stream-experts` read the wrong shard for layers past a shard boundary (NaN logits from layer 13 on, Swift 1.5). An A750 prompt of 2,744 tokens hung (direct copy out of pageable memory; regression test `engine/sycl/tools/test_prompt_deadlock.sh`). The first request after a start returned token 0 on `i915` when the spin bound was too short. An A770 JIT build misread memory past 4 GiB into an allocation. The xe driver aliased pages in a 22 GiB arena (NaN at layer 4). ### Mixed-IQ3 decode kernels for Battlemage (PR #4185) Packed Q2 / IQ4 lookup / IQ3_S sign arithmetic (the build option) and fourteen decode controls. Measured on two Arc Pro B65 (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GSQ-RCO IQ3_S, all experts resident, layer split, `--spec 2 --pipeline-windows 2`, int8 KV, AOT bmg-g31): decode +9.7% on a 4K prompt and +11.1% on a free-form answer against the build without them, same generated tokens, same logprobs to six decimals. Prompt speed is unchanged. * `STRATA_SYCL_IQ_DECODE_FAST` (CMake, default ON; `IQ_DECODE_FAST=OFF` for `engine/sycl/tools/build.sh` and `tools/packaging/build_sycl_linux.sh`): integer arithmetic with the same results as the helpers it replaces. It is the largest part of the gain (+5.9% alone). * Runtime controls. Unset: on for a Battlemage device, off for every other device (Arc A-series keeps the earlier kernels). `STRATA_<name>=0` turns a control off, `=1` turns it on whatever the device. Restart after changing one. | Runtime control | On by default (Battlemage) | Selected work | |---|---|---| | `STRATA_MMVQ_SHAPE_RPW` | yes | Row reuse for bounded Q4_K/Q5_K projection shapes | | `STRATA_IQ3S_GU_ROW_REUSE` | yes | Reuse IQ3_S gate/up row inputs across two rows | | `STRATA_IQ2S_GU_ROW_REUSE` | yes | The same for IQ2_S | | `STRATA_IQ3XXS_GU_ROW_REUSE` | yes | The same for IQ3_XXS | | `STRATA_GR_LO_REUSE` | yes | Reuse the hyper-connection low-rank SiLU output on supported layouts | | `STRATA_ATTN_MERGE_ACTIVE` | yes | Merge only the active chunks in bounded batched QSA decode | | `STRATA_IQ3S_GU_SLM` | no | Stage native IQ3_S gate/up activations (unreachable while the IQ3_S row reuse is on) | | `STRATA_IQ4NL_DOWN_SLM` | no | Stage native IQ4_NL down activations | | `STRATA_EXPERT_ROW_E3` | no | Three-entry tails in the IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS row-reuse path | | `STRATA_RESIDENT_PLAN_COMPACT` | no | Size the resident routing work-group for the entry count | | `STRATA_GR_CACHED_NORM` | no | Reuse the hyper-connection normalized input on supported layouts | | `STRATA_GR_REDUCE_ILP` | no | Keep partial loads in flight in the cached-lo hyper-connection reduce | | `STRATA_Q6_SHAPE_GRF` | no | Large GRF for bounded Q6_K projection shapes | | `STRATA_GDN_QK_REG` | no | Register-broadcast QK for supported Battlemage GDN geometry | The eight "no" controls measured neutral or slightly slower on that configuration (an internal measurement; the single-control table is not published); they stay available for other models and cards. Unsupported layouts retain their existing paths. Explicit projection overrides take precedence over shape selection. # Intel Arc on Linux Strata runs on Intel Arc cards on Linux through its own engine ported to SYCL (Intel oneAPI). This page is for people with an Arc A-series (Alchemist) or B-series (Battlemage) card. It covers the released Terminal route, what you need, how to build the engine from source, and which cards were tested. The port's workflow and measurements are in [INTEL.md](INTEL.md). maxfridbe wrote the port in [#423](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/pull/423). The code is in `sycl/`. Intel Arc is an official platform since 0.1.40.2. The maintainers test on an Arc Pro B70 (32 GB, `xe` driver) and an Arc A750 (8 GB, `i915` driver); results from other cards are community reports. The Mac and Windows builds have no Intel engine. ## Quick start Install the [Terminal](INSTALL.md#the-terminal), then point `strata launch` at the folder that holds the model's `.gguf` files (the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next files from ISTA-DASLab, for example IQ3_S or IQ2_XS): ```sh strata launch --model-path /path/to/the/gguf/folder --plan # shows what would happen, changes nothing strata launch --model-path /path/to/the/gguf/folder ``` The first launch does everything itself: it downloads the Intel engine package `linux-x86_64-sycl` from the signed feed, builds the pack for your model from the GGUF files (a few minutes, once), writes the run settings and starts the server. Nothing is installed by hand. - **A PC with an NVIDIA or AMD card as well** uses that card by default, and `--plan` says the Intel cards exist. To use the Intel cards add `--backend intel` once: the choice is remembered (in the settings file) for the next launch, `strata update` and the app's engine check. `strata launch --backend auto` goes back to the PC's own choice. Nothing is refused either way. - **Models are not downloaded for Intel cards yet.** Give the folder with `--model-path`; Strata does not touch your files. - **The draft layer (MTP) is not built for Intel cards**, so answers are a little slower than on a card with the full setup. An existing `mtp/rt` folder in the data folder is used. - `strata doctor --live` checks the driver, the render group and the card, and `strata update --check` shows the engine package. On Linux, `strata update` (Terminal) and Settings > Update (app) download the Intel engine package for a PC whose graphics card is made by Intel. One package serves Alchemist and Battlemage: the GPU code is compiled from SPIR-V at the first start, because the A-series cards have no FP64 units. The package carries oneAPI's runtime libraries. The Level Zero loader and the compute runtime stay the PC's own (see [What you need](#what-you-need)), and your user must be in the `render` group (`strata doctor` says so). It was tested on an Arc A750 and, in 0.2.10, on two Arc Pro B65 cards. The package is built by `tools/packaging/build_sycl_linux.sh`. The source and container workflow ([INTEL.md](INTEL.md#setup)) still exists for building the engine yourself; the Terminal does not need it. Docker: the ready-made image is `ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-sycl`, published only for a release that carries a Linux Intel engine package. Otherwise [build the image yourself](DOCKER.md#build-it-yourself). The image needs prepared model files ([Docker: Intel Arc](DOCKER.md#intel-arc)). ## What you need - **Linux**, for example Ubuntu 24.04, with Intel's GPU driver: the `xe` or `i915` kernel driver plus the compute runtime and Level Zero. On Ubuntu: `intel-opencl-icd libze1 libze-intel-gpu1`, or follow Intel's [client GPU guide](https://dgpu-docs.intel.com/driver/client/overview.html). - **The CPU and the model folder.** The CPU does not need AVX-512. A Ryzen 3000-5000 or an Intel Core 12th-14th generation runs the experts that do not fit on the card with AVX2 (measured on an A750 with a Ryzen 5 5600X, [INTEL.md](INTEL.md)). This applies to model folders that contain `native_experts.txt` (IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, NVFP4, Unsloth). An older Q2_0 folder has no such file, and its CPU kernel needs AVX-512. With that folder the engine stops with "this CPU cannot run the expert kernel", and `strata doctor` warns about it before the start. Building the model folder again with `strata setup` (or `terminal/tools/iq_pack.py`) fixes it. - For a source build without Docker: **Intel oneAPI** with the DPC++ compiler (`icpx`, **2026.1 or newer**; 2025.3 does not build the engine) and **oneMKL** (about 5 GB), `cmake` 3.24+, `ninja`, `git`, Python 3. - For `./setup.sh --backend sycl`: **Docker** and the GPU driver, nothing else from the list above. `engine/sycl/setup_intel.py` builds and runs the engine in the `strata-sycl-dev` image from `engine/sycl/tools/Dockerfile`, which starts from a community llama.cpp SYCL image (`ghcr.io/snailium/...`), not an Intel or Strata image. On Ubuntu: `sudo apt install docker.io git`, then `sudo usermod -aG docker,render $USER` and log in again. - VRAM: the port keeps the experts on the card (`--stream-experts`). A 32 GB card holds the Coder IQ1_M or IQ2_XS. Smaller cards mirror part of the experts in RAM and are slower. Under the wrapper's `STRATA_VERIFY_NO_HOST=1` there is no SSD expert tier on `xe`: every expert must be in VRAM or in the pinned RAM mirror (`STRATA_MIRROR_MIB`), and the engine refuses to start when the two do not cover the model. Size the RAM accordingly, or lower `--max-context`. ## Build with Docker (what `setup --backend sycl` uses) About 10 minutes the first time. From the checkout, called `Strata` here: ```sh cd Strata docker build --pull -t strata-sycl-dev engine/sycl/tools # once: about 6 minutes, a 13 GB image H=$(basename "$PWD") # Arc B-series: bmg-g31 (Pro B70), bmg-g21 (B580, B570, Pro B60). Arc A-series (Alchemist): leave out AOT (JIT) and use build-sycl docker run --rm -u $(id -u):$(id -g) -v "$PWD/..:/work" -e AOT=bmg-g31 -e REPO=/work/$H \ -e BUILD_DIR=/work/$H/build-sycl-aot strata-sycl-dev "cd /work/$H && bash engine/sycl/tools/build.sh strata" ``` `--pull` matters: [INTEL.md](INTEL.md#how-to-build-it) says why. Then run `./setup.sh --backend sycl`. Do not run `python3 engine/sycl/setup_intel.py` by hand: on Ubuntu it fails with `externally-managed-environment`; `setup.sh` runs it in its own `.venv`. ## Build without Docker This builds the engine for running it by hand ([INTEL.md](INTEL.md#how-to-run-it-by-hand)). `setup` itself uses the Docker build. Install oneAPI from Intel's apt repository: ```sh wget -qO- https://apt.repos.intel.com/intel-gpg-keys/GPG-PUB-KEY-INTEL-SW-PRODUCTS.PUB \ | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/oneapi-archive-keyring.gpg echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/oneapi-archive-keyring.gpg] https://apt.repos.intel.com/oneapi all main" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/oneAPI.list sudo apt update sudo apt install intel-oneapi-compiler-dpcpp-cpp intel-oneapi-mkl-devel ninja-build cmake git ``` Build the engine through the top-level CMake option or by configuring the `sycl/` project directly: ```sh source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh cmake -S engine -B build-sycl -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=icx -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=icpx -DSTRATA_ENABLE_SYCL=ON # or: cmake -S engine/sycl -B build-sycl -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=icx -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=icpx cmake --build build-sycl --target strata ``` | Option | Effect | | --- | --- | | `-DSTRATA_SYCL_AOT=bmg-g31` | Compile ahead of time for Arc Pro B70. Needs `ocloc` (Intel's `intel-ocloc` package). Without it the first start JIT-compiles every kernel (about 47 s). | | `-DSTRATA_SYCL_AOT=bmg-g21` | The same for B580, B570 and Pro B60 | | `-DSTRATA_SYCL_PARITY=OFF` | Skip the kernel tests (on by default). Run them with `ctest --test-dir build-sycl` on the card. | `setup_intel.py` looks for `build-sycl-aot/strata` or `build-sycl/strata` in the checkout. With the top-level option the engine is at `build-sycl/sycl/strata`, so use `-S sycl` or set `STRATA_SYCL_BIN`. ## Setup and running ```sh ./setup.sh --backend sycl [setup's usual options, e.g. --model IQ2_XS --context 32768] ``` Setup continues with `engine/sycl/setup_intel.py`, which finds the Arc in sysfs, uses the SYCL engine you built, and writes the config and `run-<model>.sh`. On a card under 12 GB or an `i915` card (the A-series) it writes the small-card config ([INTEL.md](INTEL.md#arc-a750-and-the-other-alchemist-cards)). It downloads and packs the model the usual way. Windows has no path: `setup --backend sycl` on Windows stops and points here. Things that matter on an Arc (details in [INTEL.md](INTEL.md)): - **Do not ask for more VRAM than the card has.** On the `xe` driver an allocation past VRAM can push buffers into RAM until the machine runs out of memory and stalls. Leave about 1.5 GB free. - `SYCL_CACHE_PERSISTENT=0`: the persistent JIT cache crashed on Xe2 during the first compile. - Two cards: `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:*` (the image pins `level_zero:0`; `strata-sycl.sh` passes the variable through) and `--layer-split`. - `--layer-split auto` on two equal cards takes the split that leaves the fullest card the most VRAM to spare, within 0.2% of the best predicted time (`STRATA_SPLIT_HEADROOM_TOL`). `STRATA_SPLIT_HEADROOM=0` turns that off. A full card under `xe` moves buffers to system memory instead of failing. The startup line names both splits when the choice moves. - **Two Arc B-series cards decode faster by default.** With exactly two B-series cards (B50, B60, B65, B70, B570, B580) in a layer split, the first card starts the next window while the second still checks this one (`--pipeline-windows 2`), and setup writes `--spec 2` for the pair. On 2x Arc Pro B65 this decodes 17% to 23% faster than the old serial `--spec 4` setup, 5 pairs out of 5: chat 71-74 tok/s against 60-63, JSON 80-83 against 67-68, code 72-78 against 59-65, plain text 67-68 against 56-57. The answers are those of a serial `--spec 2` run (100 of 100 agent requests); a serial `--spec 4` run differs in a rare near-tie (3 of 100). One card, an A-series card, a mixed pair and three or more cards run as before. `--pipeline-windows 0` turns it off, and a `--spec` of your own, put in the config's `user_args`, is kept. - **Arc Pro B60:** PCI id `8086:e211` (`lspci -nn`), `sycl-ls` prints `Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics 20.1.0`, so `-DSTRATA_SYCL_AOT=bmg-g21` is the right target. `setup_intel.py` knows both B60 ids, `e211` and `e221`. On a `--layer-split` the startup line "N experts are neither in VRAM nor mirrored" counts the other card's layers; read the following `100% of the experts resident` lines. Set `STRATA_MIRROR_MIB=0` there, or the pinned mirror is allocated and not used. - **`setvars.sh` and `set -u`:** `source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh` in a shell with `set -u` stops at `OCL_ICD_FILENAMES: unbound variable` (oneAPI 2026.1.1). Source it before `set -u`. - **Without Docker:** `engine/sycl/serve/strata-sycl.sh` needs Docker. Natively, `source setvars.sh`, export `SYCL_CACHE_PERSISTENT=0`, `ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1` and `STRATA_VERIFY_DEVICE_PLAN=1`, then run `build-sycl-aot/strata` or `engine/sycl/serve/server_intel.py` with an `exe` that does this. A normal user is not in the `render` group on Ubuntu, and then `sycl-ls` shows only the CPU. - `STRATA_VERIFY_NO_HOST=1` (set by `strata-sycl.sh` unless the config's `"env"` says otherwise) is needed on `xe` cards when part of the experts is not in VRAM, and is left off on the `i915` A-series ([INTEL.md](INTEL.md)). The config's `"env"` block and any `STRATA_*`, `ONEAPI_*`, `UR_*`, `IGC_*`, `SYCL_*` or `ZES_*` variable of the server's environment reach the engine through `strata-sycl.sh`. ## Tested cards > **Measured on:** the hardware in each row, Linux. Versions are the engine version of that report, not the current release. | Who | Hardware | Result | Reported in | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Port author | Arc Pro B70 32 GB, Ubuntu 24.04, 0.1.31-sycl | Coder IQ1_M: 70-78 tok/s decode, about 790 tok/s prompt; IQ2_XS: 51-64 tok/s; 256K context | #423, [INTEL.md](INTEL.md) | | Community | 2x Arc Pro B70, `--layer-split` | Flash-Next IQ3_XXS 66 tok/s decode, 394 tok/s prompt | #423 | | Community | Arc Pro B50 16 GB | Coder IQ1_M about 23 tok/s, IQ2_XS about 25-27 tok/s, up to 128K | #423 | | Community | Arc B580 12 GB, WSL2 | IQ2_XS about 21 tok/s, Coder about 15 tok/s; device loss also seen | #423 | | Community | 2x Arc Pro B60 24 GB, `--layer-split`, Ryzen 5 5600, 64 GB, PCIe 3.0 x8 per card | Coder IQ1_M: 56.6 tok/s decode, 428 tok/s prompt (2,129 tokens); Flash-Next IQ2_XS: 58.6-61.3 tok/s decode, 436 tok/s prompt; all experts in VRAM; 8K context | [report](bench-results/2026-10-04-community-2x-arc-pro-b60/README.md) | | Community | One Arc Pro B60 24 GB | Coder IQ1_M with 4,042 of 12,288 experts mirrored in RAM: 11.9 tok/s decode | same | | Maintainers | Arc Pro B70 32 GB (xe), 0.1.40.2 and later | Flash-Next IQ3_S with 11.5k of 24.6k experts resident: 10-prompt gate passes, prompt 980-1,000 tok/s on 4K tokens, decode 30 (prose) to 41 (code) tok/s | [INTEL.md](INTEL.md#arc-pro-b70-with-a-model-that-does-not-fit-flash-next-iq3_s) | | Maintainers | Arc A750 8 GB (i915) | Flash-Next IQ3_XXS about 10-19 tok/s decode | [INTEL.md](INTEL.md#arc-a750-and-the-other-alchemist-cards) | | Maintainers | 2x Arc Pro B65 32 GB (xe), 0.2.8 | Flash-Next IQ3_S, every expert in VRAM, the JIT package build: decode 71-83 tok/s (chat, JSON, code), prompts 1,261 / 1,511 / 1,628 tok/s at 4K / 8K / 16K | the bullet above | Two cards on `xe` (2x Arc Pro B70, IQ3_S, 0.1.44): `--layer-split auto` picked a split at about 11 tok/s where `--layer-split 30` ran about 54. The auto choice now prefers the split with the most VRAM headroom (above). **Not tested by anyone:** Windows (no native build path), Arc on WSL2 with the current engine, integrated Arc GPUs (the B390 / Panther Lake in #515; shared-memory planning does not exist), and pictures on a Battlemage card with a GPU reader. Pictures work on the A750 (on by default, read on the CPU). See [INTEL.md](INTEL.md#pictures-on-an-arc). ## Windows There is no Windows path. `setup --backend sycl` on Windows stops and points here. oneAPI exists for Windows, but `engine/sycl/CMakeLists.txt` uses GCC-style flags (`-mavx512f`, `-fp-model=precise`, `-qmkl`) and the runner is a bash/Docker script. Nobody has tried a native build. WSL2 with an Arc was used by one tester (the B580 row above), but setup cannot detect the card there, because it reads `/sys/class/drm`, which WSL2 does not have. ## Reporting a problem Open an issue with the card, the driver version, the `sycl-ls` output, the oneAPI version, the model and flags, and the engine's stderr. Results from real cards are what move more cards from tested to validated. ## History / older measurements The first port (0.1.39) compiled with 0 errors on Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2) with oneAPI DPC++ 2026.1.1 and oneMKL 2026.1: the `strata` engine plus 157 targets, as SPIR-V (JIT). No one ran an unpatched 0.1.39 port on an Arc; the other rows were measured on earlier versions. # Strata engine and server reference This page is the technical reference for the Qwen engine and its server: measured speed, the HTTP API, the settings in `strata-<model>.json`, memory modes and the speed switches. It is for people who run Strata from a source checkout, tune an installation or connect their own software. It describes the current release. The default address is `http://127.0.0.1:8080`: ```sh curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "strata", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about GPUs."}], "max_tokens": 512}' ``` 3. Setup rewrites the file when you run it again and keeps the keys it does not manage. --- <a id="speed-measured"></a> ## Speed (measured) **Measured on:** RTX 5070 12 GB, Ryzen 5 7600 (6 cores), 64 GB DDR5-5200, Windows, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ISTA-DASLab packs, engine 0.1.26 with the settings setup writes (`--prefill auto`, 8-bit KV above 4K, KV streaming from 64K). One code-agent prompt per length, 256 generated tokens, MTP speculative decoding on. "262K" is the full context window (a 259,943-token prompt). The IQ2_XS row used Swift 1.5's IQ2_XS, which runs at the original's speed. ### Prompt processing (tokens/s) | Model | 1K | 4K | 32K | 64K | 128K | 262K | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | **Q2_0** | 536 | 1,299 | 2,171 | 2,126 | 2,107 | 1,304† | | **IQ2_XS** | 534 | 1,256 | 2,092 | 1,754 | 1,752 | 1,181*† | | **IQ3_XXS** | 482 | 1,007 | 1,745 | 1,609 | 1,602 | - | | **IQ3_S** | 427 | 913 | 1,624 | 1,640 | 1,443 | - | | **Coder** | 656 | 1,583 | 2,177 | 2,236 | 2,208 | 1,034** | † not measured again since 0.1.22. \* measured with images on (the image encoder's VRAM reserve leaves fewer experts cached). \*\* not measured again since 0.1.14. ### Output (tokens/s) | Model | 1K | 4K | 32K | 64K | 128K | 262K | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | **Q2_0** | 87.3 | 93.0 | 81.8 | 76.2 | 73.7 | 60.3† | | **IQ2_XS** | 79.6 | 78.6 | 76.3 | 63.7 | 62.7 | 52.8† | | **IQ3_XXS** | 61.9 | 61.6 | 58.5 | 57.2 | 49.0 | - | | **IQ3_S** | 52.4 | 53.3 | 48.3 | 46.3 | 45.5 | - | | **Coder** | 58.9 | 55.1 | 54.9 | 53.2 | 43.0 | 42.8† | † not measured again since 0.1.14. Raw data: `docs/bench-results/2026-09-29-speed-0126`. - Output speed depends on the text. Speculative decoding runs faster when more drafted tokens are accepted, so a different answer to the same prompt moves it by several percent. - Time to first token is prompt length divided by prompt speed. With Q2_0 that is about 4 s at 4K, 25 s at 32K, under 2 minutes at 128K and 4.5 minutes at 262K. - IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S at 262K are not measured. With 43 and 50 GB of experts, a 260K-token context brings a 64 GB PC to its memory limit by setup's estimate, so setup recommends up to 128K there. A longer context that you choose is kept, with a note. - Other cards, other CPUs and newer engines differ. The 0.1.36 fused prompt kernels and later changes raised these numbers on RTX 30 and newer cards: see [History](#history--older-measurements). For your own PC, run the benchmark in [BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md](BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md). More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU. Every extra GB holds about 700 more experts, and every expert on the GPU is one the CPU does not have to compute. `terminal/tools/make_profile.py` builds an expert profile from your own prompts: run the engine once with `--dump-routing trace.bin`, then see the tool's help. The shipped profile ranks every expert pair, so a trace changes the order only with `--reorder` (your trace's pairs first, then the base's, then the rest). ## Which model? [MODELS.md](MODELS.md) is the page for choosing a model: sizes, memory, providers and what fits. The families are Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (with its Coder, Swift, Gyro, Unsloth and NVFP4 variants) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ([QWEN36.md](QWEN36.md)). The ISTA-DASLab Qwen3.8-Flash-Next packs are: | Model | Download | RAM it uses | Speed | Quality | | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | | **Q2_0** | 66 GB | ~34 GB experts + ~6 GB | fastest | good | | **IQ2_XS** | 68 GB | ~36 GB experts + ~6 GB | close to Q2_0 | a bit better | | **IQ3_XXS** | 76 GB | ~43 GB experts + ~6 GB | slower (more CPU work) | best of the three | IQ3_S is a fourth, larger pack: see [MODELS.md](MODELS.md#pick-by-memory). What it does and the manual workflow are in [UNSLOTH_Q4.md](UNSLOTH_Q4.md). --- ## Windows On Windows the source wrapper is `START-HERE.bat` ([source installation](SOURCE_INSTALL.md#from-source-windows)). For a released app, run its installer and open Strata from the Start menu. For the Terminal, use `strata launch`. Watch the setup plan and the startup log for what is actually chosen on your machine, and see [TROUBLESHOOTING.md](TROUBLESHOOTING.md) if a component is missing. Terminal chat from a checkout: `terminal\.venv\Scripts\python terminal\tools\chat.py`. ### Tuning for your PC (`--calibrate`) Some engine settings depend on the PC more than on the model: | Setting | What it controls | | --- | --- | | `--pcie-frac` | Share of the experts missing from VRAM that are copied to the GPU instead of computed by the CPU. A fast PCIe link and a slow CPU want more; a laptop's narrow link wants less. | | `--spec-min-p` | How sure the draft layer must be to add another guess to a check. | | `--pool-workers` | How many CPU threads compute experts. On CPUs with efficiency cores, fewer can be faster. | | `--adapt-every`, `--adapt-swaps`, `--adapt-decay` | How busily the VRAM expert cache follows the conversation. A CPU that reads missed experts slowly (DDR3 or DDR4 in few channels) gains from more swaps. | | `--prefill-pipe` | On two or more cards (layer split), the prompt chunks that keep the cards reading at once. See [MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md). | The defaults were measured on a Ryzen 5 7600 with an RTX 5070. From a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --calibrate` (Linux: `./setup.sh --calibrate`) measures output speed with each setting on your PC and keeps one only when it is more than 3% faster. The result is remembered per PC and model, and updates keep it. Measuring the worker count restarts the model more than once, so the PC is busy and can stop responding for a minute or two at each restart. ### Running it at startup (Task Scheduler) To have the model up at logon, start the server from Task Scheduler or a service. Windows throttles such contexts by default, and the expert load then crawls. **Measured on:** RTX 5070 Ti, Ryzen 7 9800X3D, NVMe, a ~40 GB expert load, same binary, arguments and cache state. | How the server starts | Expert load | | --- | ---: | | Double-click, terminal or SSH | 1.42-1.52 GiB/s (~35 s) | | Task Scheduler with its defaults | 0.05 GiB/s (821-841 s) | | Task Scheduler with the two settings below | 1.42 GiB/s (35 s) | In the task's properties set both of these (the defaults are the opposite): - **Priority level: Normal** (Options tab; the default is Below normal). - **Run with highest privileges** (General tab). Without it the task runs with a limited token, which also removes `SeLockMemoryPrivilege`, the privilege Windows large pages need. Both were changed at once, so the effect of each alone is not measured. If the model still starts slowly, the engine prints a hint under its `loaded ... GiB at ...` line. **Large pages need a new logon.** Granting "Lock pages in memory" (`secpol.msc`, User Rights Assignment) to the account that runs the engine takes effect at the next logon. Log off and on after granting it. Until then the startup log says large pages were refused. `terminal\tools\windows\enable_large_pages.ps1` (run as Administrator) grants it to the current account. --- ## Linux These notes are for **source setup**. Normal installs use [the Terminal or AppImage](INSTALL.md). ```bash ./setup.sh ``` Source setup offers choices for the detected machine and can install missing Debian or Ubuntu dependencies with `sudo apt`. It starts the server on `http://127.0.0.1:8080` unless you configure another address or port. Later runs of `./setup.sh` or `./run-<model>.sh` start the model directly. The options are the same as on Windows (`./setup.sh --setup`, `--model Q2_0 --yes`, `--gguf-dir /data/Q2_0`). Terminal chat: `terminal/.venv/bin/python terminal/tools/chat.py`. Building from git and trying a pull request: [SOURCE_INSTALL.md](SOURCE_INSTALL.md#build-from-git-on-linux-to-try-a-pull-request-or-change-the-code). - **Updating:** `git pull`, then `./setup.sh`. It compiles the engine again when its source changed. If the compile fails, it says so and starts the engine you had. - **Other distributions** (Arch, Fedora and others): install the C++ compiler and the CUDA Toolkit 13 with your package manager first (Arch: `sudo pacman -S base-devel cuda`). Setup finds `nvcc` on `PATH`, in `/usr/local/cuda*` and in `/opt/cuda*`. - **WSL** works (Ubuntu 24.04 tested) with one limit. The NVIDIA driver pins only about 1 GB there, so KV streaming (`--kv-resident`) is off, the KV cache stays in VRAM and experts are copied from unpinned RAM, which makes prompts slower than on native Linux. --- ### Downloading the model files yourself Setup downloads the model files over 16 connections (`STRATA_DL_CONNECTIONS` 1 to 32), resumes a stopped download, and checks every file's SHA-256 against the pinned value. Measured from two computers (a home PC and a server in China), anonymous downloads from Hugging Face ran at 16 to 19 MB/s whatever the connection count (one stream 7 MB/s, 16 connections 17, 32 connections 19). Hugging Face's own `hf` command with its Xet backend gave 16 to 24 MB/s anonymously in the same test, so it is not faster by itself. Hugging Face limits anonymous requests per IP address and says a login (a token of your own account) raises the limits, so if the download is slow you can fetch the file with the `hf` command, optionally after `hf auth login`, and give the folder to setup: ```bash uvx hf auth login # optional: your own Hugging Face account; Strata does not read or send this token uvx hf download agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf \ --revision 1ada08422e404aca51ab9df665f089f34c419c6b --local-dir /data/gyro-s ./setup.sh --gguf-dir /data/gyro-s # Windows: SETUP.bat --gguf-dir D:\gyro-s ``` Use the file names and the revision setup shows for your model (the revision above is the one this version pins for Gyro-S: another version of Strata may pin another). Keep the file's original name. Setup finds the files in `--gguf-dir`, checks their SHA-256 and does not download them again; a file that does not match the published one is reported and, for files in your own folder, never deleted. Without `uvx`, `pip install -U huggingface_hub` gives the same `hf` command. ### Installing a model from another program (`--output jsonl`) A program that installs a model for its user (`setup.py --yes --no-start --family F --model M --data-dir D`) can add `--output jsonl`. Setup then writes one JSON object per line to stdout and nothing else: its usual text, and the output of every program it runs, goes to stderr. The exit codes stay the same. Every object has `"schema_version": 1` and an `"event"`: | `event` | Other fields | Sent when | | --- | --- | --- | | `step` | `n`, `title` | a numbered step starts (`=== Step N: ... ===` in the text) | | `ok` | `message` | a check passed or a part is ready (an `[ok]` line) | | `warning` | `message` | setup goes on but says something (a `[!]` line) | | `progress` | `label`, `done_bytes`, `total_bytes` | during a download: at most once a second per file, and once at the end | | `error` | `message`, `hint` (or null), `exit_code`; `kind` for some stops | setup stops, just before it exits with `exit_code`. `kind` is `no_space` (with `path`, `free_bytes`, `needed_bytes`) when the disk is too full, `refused` when the install would need a download it may not make, `interrupted` after Ctrl+C | | `done` | `exit_code`, `run_config` | the last line of a run that ends by itself: `run_config` is the absolute path of the `strata-<model>.json` setup wrote (null if it wrote none) | New fields may be added to an event; a reader should ignore fields it does not know. ## Memory modes ### KV cache | Option | What it does | | --- | --- | | `--kv int8` (default) | 8-bit KV cache. | | `--kv q4_0` | Half the KV memory with a Hadamard rotation before 4-bit rounding. About 4% faster at 128K, measurably less precise on long documents (perplexity +8-12%; needle tests still pass). Setup asks above 8K context. | | `--kv k8v4` | Keys at 8 bits, values as rotated 4-bit: 23% less KV memory than 8-bit, so more experts fit in VRAM. More precise than `q4_0` on long documents. Prompts are 2-5% slower. | | `--kv-streaming on\|off\|auto` | Keeps the context's KV cache in RAM and only the part attention reads in VRAM (`--kv-resident 32768`), so more experts fit on the GPU. Costs about 13.7 KB of RAM per context token (1.7 GB at 128K). Setup turns it on from 64K when the RAM has room; `on` overrides the RAM test with a note. Never under WSL. | | `--kv-grow` (or `STRATA_KV_GROW=1`; `--no-kv-grow` turns it off) | The KV takes VRAM only for the cells the requests reach; the expert cache holds the rest and gives slots back as the context grows. Needs one GPU, an expert profile, the whole KV in VRAM and every expert in RAM. Otherwise the engine says so and stays off. On HIP it uses virtual memory management (`STRATA_HIP_VMM=0` turns that off). It pays on cards of about 24 GB or less with contexts of 128K and more. | `STRATA_KV_HOST_REGISTER=1` forces the KV host copy to be pinned with `cudaHostRegister` (the order WSL2 uses automatically); `0` forces `cudaHostAlloc` first. ### Low-RAM modes (chosen by setup) Normally all of a model's experts are copied into RAM (23-50 GB, pinned) and the GPU holds a copy of the most-used ones. When the RAM cannot hold them beside the system (the experts plus about 10 GB), setup picks one of these: | Mode | Flag | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | Mapped | `--mmap-experts` | Maps the experts from one file in the model's folder (the pack's `experts.bin`, +23-50 GB of disk), or from the GGUF files themselves for native packs that have no `experts.bin`. The OS file cache holds what the GPU does not and can give that memory back. With a small GPU most experts come from the SSD and it is much slower; setup says so. | | Resident | `--resident-experts` | When the experts the GPU does not hold fit the RAM, the engine copies exactly those into RAM at start. Nothing is read from the SSD while it answers. | | RAM budget | `--resident-budget-gib N` | The N GiB of experts the GPU does not hold that the profile ranks hottest are copied into RAM; the rest are read from the files. Implies `--mmap-experts` and leaves 4 GiB of headroom. On Windows the available commit limit also caps N, and a clamped budget is reported. This is what runs [Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q4.md) on a 64 GB PC. | - In a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --setup --low-ram on|off` overrides the choice, and `--low-ram resident|mmap` forces one variant. - The resident variant keeps 4 GB of the RAM it finds free (`STRATA_RESIDENT_HEADROOM_GIB`). When even the missing experts do not fit, it says so and runs the mapped mode. The server log shows per request how many expert reads went to the file (`resident RAM: ... blob reads from the file`, 0 in steady use). - The adaptive tier (`--adapt-every`) keeps following the conversation in the resident mode. `--adapt-async 1` (opt-in, `--serve`) moves the swaps between decode windows on a helper thread. With `--batch` slots it works between their windows too, but not with `--batch-groups` or `--peer-device`. It is not bit-exact from run to run. - `STRATA_RAM_ADAPT=<n>` (opt-in, `--serve`, one GPU, needs `--adapt-every`): the RAM copy also follows the conversation. A layer swaps up to 4 pairs per window: the experts the windows keep routing to (decayed count 2 or more) take the RAM places of unused experts of the same layer (count below 0.5), largest difference first. The incoming expert was usually read for the window before; when its blob still sits in that read's stage buffer it is copied from there and no file read is made. `n` caps only the pairs that need a file read (`=1` is enough in practice). The log counts how many experts moved and how many came out of a stage buffer. - Several GPUs: setup recommends one GPU in the low-RAM mode and asks. `--gpus 0,1` shares the model across both cards ([MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md#using-it)). `--yes` keeps one GPU. - With a page-locked copy the GPU also takes its share of the misses over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). `--pcie-frac 0` (or `STRATA_RESIDENT_PIN=0`) gives the mapped mode's exact tokens. `STRATA_RESIDENT_PIN=0` applies to `--resident-experts`, `--resident-budget-gib N` and the RAM copy the engine makes on its own when the expert arena does not fit. - Linux, opt-in: `STRATA_ARENA_MMAP=1` maps a native pack's expert arena read-only from `experts.bin` instead of reading it into locked RAM (for example 2x 16 GB GPUs with 32 GB of RAM). Run it with `--pcie-frac 0`. - Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_FILE_RELEASE=1` trims the file-backed pages of experts after their GPU uploads. It is a working-set hint, not an unmap, and it does not reduce committed memory or SSD reads ([measurements and limits](bench-results/2026-10-04-windows-mapped-release/README.md)). - Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_PIN_BY_NEED=1` (arena on one GPU) registers the profile's non-GPU-resident experts by rank up to `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` (29 by default on Windows) instead of the first ~30 GiB. - Windows CUDA keeps 640 MiB then 160 MiB of page-lockable memory free while the arena pins (`STRATA_PIN_RESERVE_MIB=N`, `0` turns it off, and it sets the reserve on any OS). If a required buffer is still refused, the error ends with `[pinned-memory-exhausted]` and names the `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` to start with. - `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1` (opt-in): an adaptive swap hands buffer ownership over instead of copying the evicted blob into the RAM copy. Same tokens, fewer host copies, about 1.4 GiB more page-locked RAM. See [EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md](EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md). ### Linux file tier When experts are read from GGUF files in place, Linux runs three things by default. Off switches are in brackets. | Part | Variable | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | Zero-copy | `STRATA_COLD_OVERLAP=4` (`0` = off) | An expert whose three tensors' pages are all in the page cache is computed straight from the mapping, with no staging copy. | | io prefetch | `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` (`0` = off) | I/O threads read the layer's uncached experts and the router-predicted ones of the next layers with whole-blob `pread`s into the page cache. Tunables: `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_K`, `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH_DEPTH` (2), `STRATA_IO_PF_THREADS` (8), `STRATA_IO_PF_STAGE=1`, `STRATA_IO_PF_AHEAD=0`. | | Decode gate | `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE=1` (`0` = off) | Every 16 decode windows the read-ahead is judged. It runs only while the page cache has room for the experts (off below 0.55, on above 0.65: `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE_LO` and `_HI`) and while it pays (`STRATA_IO_PF_GATE_USEFUL`). | A closure for low prefetch benefit retries after 256 decode windows while capacity stays at or above the low watermark. A capacity drop below that watermark cancels the retry; reopening then requires the high watermark to be exceeded. For an `experts.bin` pack, io prefetch and the gate switch on when the page cache has room for at least 55% of the experts (the tightest cgroup limit or `MemAvailable`, asked once at start). Below that the pack reads as before and the log says so; `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` forces it. The container RAM check counts a cgroup's clean page cache as available. The startup log names what is on. When every expert is in the GPU caches (the decode reads nothing from the file tier) the defaults, the decode gate and the routing-aware prefetch are off, and they come back when a request starts with fewer experts held (a VRAM resize, an eviction); `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` keeps io prefetch and the look-ahead, `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD=1` keeps the look-ahead, `STRATA_FILE_TIER_IDLE=0` turns this off. Windows and macOS are unchanged. On a Radeon 780M iGPU, prefetch together with the adaptive tier under memory pressure reset the GPU in most runs; with `--adapt-every 100000` there were none, and the cause is not found. The weights and the MTP draft files are asked for ahead of their reads at start (madvise and `posix_fadvise` WILLNEED, 128 KiB steps), which matters on a slow drive: `STRATA_READ_AHEAD=0` turns it off, `STRATA_FILL_AHEAD=N` sets how many fill pairs are requested ahead (default 256). **Sequential read-ahead on the mapped experts (Linux, opt-in).** `STRATA_EXPERTS_SEQ_READAHEAD=1` marks the mapped expert files (`experts.bin`, or the GGUF shards in place) `MADV_SEQUENTIAL` when they are mapped. When the experts outside the GPU are much larger than the file cache, the kernel can stop reading ahead on the mapping: each page fault then reads one 4 KiB page, and a prompt waits on hundreds of thousands of small reads. With the variable each fault reads the drive's read-ahead window. The answers are the same. Measured on one PC: RX 6900 XT 16 GB, Ryzen 9 9950X, 32 GB RAM, Gyro-M (a 29.9 GiB `experts.bin` on two NVMe SSDs in RAID0), Linux 7.2, `--adapt-swaps 0`, a cold page cache before each run, the same binary with and without the variable (2 runs without, 4 with): | | Without | With | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Five follow-up turns of 650 to 970 new tokens | 65.2 / 76.2 s | 23.5 to 28.4 s | | One follow-up turn | 5.7 to 28.6 s | 4.4 to 6.3 s | | Major page faults in one follow-up turn | 15,000 to 1,350,000 | 73,000 to 115,000 | | A 20K-token first prompt | 31.0 / 31.9 s | 23.9 to 32.4 s | | An 800-token answer at 24K context | 32.8 / 43.9 tok/s | 42.0 to 52.2 tok/s | Without the variable a turn took about 6 s while the kernel kept reading ahead (about 15,000 faults) and 15 to 29 s once it stopped (0.5 to 1.35 million); in two more runs without it the first prompt took 28.6 s with 60,000 faults and 120.5 s with 7.6 million. With adaptive swaps on (the default) that PC stopped long sessions with and without the variable (#4566), so these runs had them off. Not measured: a PC whose file cache holds the experts, a slower drive (the decode's scattered misses also read a whole window there). The prompt chunk follows the host's memory (Linux, file tier, on by default). When the page cache is smaller than the file set, a planner picks the chunk and ring with the fewest predicted bytes read per prompt from the RAM copy, the page cache that is left, the drive class and the PCIe link. It prints `chunk 8192 -> 3840, ring 96 -> 96: ...` when it changes the pick and `chunk 8192 kept: ...` when it does not. It does nothing when the GPU holds every expert, when the file set fits the cache, and on Windows. `STRATA_PREFILL_HOST_PLAN=0` turns it off; `STRATA_SSD_GBPS` overrides the drive speed; `--prefill N` and `STRATA_PREFILL_RING` always win. ### Reading the tiers With `--stats` the engine prints the tiers of the decode (`expert tiers`: blobs from the RAM copy, blobs and MB from the files, read time; `routing prefetch`: how many file reads had been warmed). The server log has the same per request, and `GET /metrics` lists `ram_blobs`, `file_blobs`, `file_mb`, `drafts_offered` and `drafts_accepted` per recent request, with `totals` since the start. `hit_rate` is the VRAM share of the experts looked up; experts the GPU reads over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`) are not in it, so a higher `--pcie-frac` raises it even when decoding gets slower. `pcie_share` is their share of all routed experts. The Monitor tab shows both. The request list in the Monitor tab also shows the prompt's own speed: what the cache already held is not read again, so it is the fresh tokens (`prompt_tokens` minus `reused`) over the prompt time (`prompt_ms`), and a request that read no new token shows no number. Profiling: start the server with `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` (and `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1` for the GPU side). After each request the engine log has a `strata decode timing:` line and a `strata decode GPU stages (ms/window):` line. The GPU profile slows decoding a little: use it to compare, not to measure speed. `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_STATS=1` scores the next-layer expert prediction every 100 windows and costs CPU. `terminal/tools/replay_cache_policy.py` replays a `--dump-routing` trace through the adaptive tier's swap policy offline. In the serial serve loop the timing line lists the wall-time parts in the order they run: `adapt wait + verify + commit/emit + draft + adapt join + other`. `other` is the decode time minus the named parts, not a step of its own. The times are host wall times, averaged over every decode window, and the bracketed parts of verify are already inside verify. The pipelined decode keeps the older line (`ms/window = verify ...`) and batch slots are not covered, so a script that reads this line must accept `ms/window = adapt wait` for a serial run. ### Draft layer | Option | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--mtp` | Use the model's MTP draft layer (setup passes it).
